chitchat: Hesketh lowers a basket into the middle fryer and the whole shop hisses.
He shakes a basket of chips, looks at them, and drops them back in for another minute.
He wraps a supper in two sheets of paper without looking down, and slides it across the counter.
"Salt and vinegar?" he asks, already doing it.
He skims the scraps off the top of the oil into the tray in the cabinet.
The swing door at the back bangs open and a box of fillets on ice comes through. He takes it without looking round.
He wipes a porthole in the steamed-up window with his sleeve and looks out at the tables.
description: A heavy man in his forties with a shaved head and forearms speckled with small white burn scars from spitting fat. He moves behind the counter without looking, and talks to the fryers more than to the customers. A pencil lives behind one ear and a tea towel over one shoulder.

bye.text: "Mind, it's hot," he says, already turning back to the fryer.

fish.text:
"Through there." He points the tongs at the swing door behind him. "Fawle lands it off the boats in the morning and it's in my batter by the afternoon. Nobody in the city eats fresher, and most of them have no idea."

"Got a catch of your own? He'll buy it. Go out the front and round to the quay, or the staff door off the car park."

good.text:
"The supper." He taps the cabinet glass over the fish. "Cod, chips, done in beef dripping, which is the only right way and costs me more than the fish does. It'll keep you going a whole shift."

"Scraps if you're broke. Nobody leaves here hungry, they just leave here with less."

late.text:
"Have to be. The Yards change shift at two, and two hundred people come off the trucks hungry. They want something they can eat in the cab out of paper. I do more between midnight and two than the whole afternoon."

"Sundays I close at ten. Even the trucks stop Sundays."

moved.text:
"Ironside, yeah. Brick place by the Meridian." He shrugs. "Fawle had a front he wasn't using and I had a delivery I was walking across town for. Now it comes through a door."

"The old unit's boarded up. Somebody'll take it. Somebody always does."

options.label: Where does the fish come from?
Didn't you used to be on Ironside Street?

root.text: "What can I get you?" He doesn't look up from the fryer.

text_by_relation.familiar: "The usual," he says, and it is not a question. He drops a fish in the batter.
text_by_relation.first:
The man behind the counter shakes a basket, hooks it on the side of the fryer and wipes his hands on the tea towel.

"Gil. Batter Days." He nods at the board. "Fish, chips, sausage, peas. Scraps are a credit if you're skint. What can I get you?"
text_by_relation.known: "Back again." He is already reaching for the paper. "Supper?"

clothing_layers: a white tunic gone cream at the cuffs
a blue-striped apron spotted with batter
black work trousers and steel-toed clogs
a paper hat folded flat in his back pocket, unworn

name: Gil Hesketh
